title: The tax collector's party (Matthew 9:9–13)
hookLine: Jesus calls Matthew from his booth and eats with his shady friends

lines: THE ONE NOBODY SITS NEXT TO.
cards: Every town has someone people avoid sitting next to. Maybe he cheated people. Maybe he works for someone everyone resents.
Maybe it's just his reputation. In Capernaum, a fishing town on the lake, there's a booth by the road where goods passing through get taxed. The man in the booth is named Matthew.

He collects money for the rulers who answer to Rome, and people assume tax collectors take extra for themselves. The Gospel doesn't say whether he did. Jesus walks past, stops, and looks right at him.

teach.b: Two words, in the King James Bible: "Follow me. And he arose, and followed him." No speech. No conditions.
Matthew gets up. Then comes the party.
Matthew opens his house for a meal, and many publicans and sinners come and sit down with Jesus and his disciples. Publican is the old word for tax collector.
Sinners here means people known for breaking the law, the ones good families kept at a distance. Some Pharisees see it.
They were serious, devout teachers who cared deeply about keeping God's law in everyday life, including who you ate with, because sharing a table meant sharing a life.
So they ask the disciples: "Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?"
It's a real question, and Jesus gives a real answer: "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick." A doctor who avoids sick people isn't much of a doctor.
Then he quotes the prophet Hosea: "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice."

teach.h: THEY THAT BE WHOLE NEED NOT A PHYSICIAN.
teach.b: Go and learn what that means, he says. And: "for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Notice where the calling happens.
Not in the temple. At a tax booth, and then at a dinner table.
In Mark and Luke the man at the booth is called Levi, and Christian tradition has long said this Matthew is the one whose name is on the first Gospel, though scholars still discuss who wrote it.
Either way, the Gospel that bears his name tells his calling in one sentence. He got up.

how: Many churches keep the feast of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, in September in the West and in November in the Orthodox calendar. Christians often point to this story when welcoming newcomers or sharing meals with people who are left out.

practice: Think about your table, whatever that means for you, your lunch spot, your group chat, the people you text back first, and then of someone who's never there: a coworker who eats alone, a neighbor you've never really met, a relative people roll their eyes at.
Picture sharing one ordinary meal with them, and what you might talk about. If you pray, you can name that person in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Publican. The old King James word for tax collector, what the crowd called Matthew before Jesus looked at him and said, follow me.

orig.note: Greek: a tax or toll collector, from telos, a tax. Matthew's job at the booth.

carryVoice: Your line: he came for the sick. Tomorrow, another party, and this time the wine runs out.
